text: 美国国家气象局伯明翰办公室发布的官方事件调查页面，专门记录 2011 年 4 月 27 日发生在阿拉巴马州 Greene、Hale 和 Bibb 三县的“Sawyerville-Eoline”龙卷风。页面给出该龙卷风的官方等级、最大风速、路径长度和宽度、起止时间与地理坐标，以及按县分段的损害叙述。文本详细描述了龙卷风自 Greene 县西南部靠近 Tombigbee 河附近触地，穿越 Black Warrior 河进入 Hale 县靠近 Sawyerville，并在 Sawyerville 附近增强为 EF3，随后进入 Talladega 国家森林，再穿过 Eoline 一带，对多处活动房屋、独立住宅、教堂以及 Eoline 消防站造成严重破坏，最终在 Bibb 县 Marvel 附近减弱并消散的过程。页面还列出伤亡人数，并说明 Greene、Hale 和 Bibb 县在 16:50 到 19:45 期间一直处于龙卷风预警之下。

Montgomery Advertiser 的龙卷风档案条目，记录 2011 年 4 月 27 日超级爆发中的一条龙卷风轨迹。搜索摘要显示，该条目描述了一条穿越 Black Warrior 河、进入 Hale 县 Sawyerville 西侧，并随后经过 Eoline 的龙卷风，并提到其造成了显著结构性损害。页面很可能以结构化形式列出该龙卷风的 EF 评级、发生时间、路径长度和宽度、影响县以及与国家气象局文本相似的路径叙述，从而为 Sawyerville–Eoline 龙卷风的地理路径和损害描述提供一份独立的新闻数据档案来源。

Tornado Talk 在其官方 Facebook 页面上发布的一则图文帖，标题和正文明确提到“Sawyerville-Eoline, AL EF3 Tornado – April 27, 2011”，并称其发布了一篇关于该事件的新免费总结文章。该贴确认 Tornado Talk 网站上存在一篇专门针对 2011 年 4 月 27 日 Sawyerville–Eoline EF3 龙卷风的详尽总结，内容可能包括时间线、路径、人员故事、照片和来源汇编。就当前素材而言，该帖主要提供事件命名方式与 EF3 等级的再次印证，并表明这一龙卷风作为独立个案被气象爱好者社区系统化记录。

YouTube 频道 “CJ Morgan – Florida Man Weather” 发布的一部长篇纪录风格视频，题为“2011 Super Outbreak”，系统回顾 2011 年超级龙卷风爆发的气象背景、各条主要龙卷风及其影响。视频章节列表中在 31:57 标注了“Sawyerville-Eoline, AL EF3”一节，表明片中单独讨论这一 EF3 级龙卷风，将其置于同一爆发中其他著名长路径龙卷风（如 Hackleburg–Phil Campbell、Cullman、Tuscaloosa–Birmingham 等）之列。该视频作为二手/三手资料，从定性角度强调 Sawyerville–Eoline 龙卷风在此次爆发中的地位和破坏程度。

Grokipedia 上关于 2011 年超级龙卷风爆发的参考性条目，汇总了此次爆发的总体规模、气象背景和统计数据。文章指出，2011 年 4 月 25–28 日期间美国共出现约 362 次确认龙卷风，涉及 21 个州，其中包括 4 条 EF5、11 条 EF4 和 21 条 EF3 龙卷风；约 321 人死亡，经济损失约 120 亿美元。4 月 27 日是爆发的峰值日，24 小时内约有 199 条龙卷风并造成 316 人死亡，主要在美国东南部。条目还描述了深槽低压、极高的墨西哥湾水汽通量、高 CAPE 和强急流等大尺度环境条件，但未对单条龙卷风（如 Sawyerville–Eoline）进行逐一命名。

al.com 于 2022 年发表的一篇回顾性特稿，纪念 2011 年 4 月 27 日阿拉巴马州的毁灭性龙卷风日。文章回顾了当天 18 小时内在阿拉巴马发生约 62 条龙卷风、造成逾 240 人死亡、总路径长度超过 1,200 英里的整体情况，并列出多条重要长路径龙卷风的关键统计数据。在“LONG-TRACK TORNADOES”部分，文章以项目符号形式给出包括 Sawyerville–Eoline 在内的多条龙卷风的路径长度、EF 等级、涉及县以及伤亡人数。对于该事件，条目写明“72.13 miles: EF-3, Sawyerville-Eoline. Greene, Hale and Bibb counties, 7 deaths, 50 injuries.”，从而以新闻媒体的形式重申并汇总官方统计。

title: Overview
content:
The 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was a long-track, violent tornado that struck portions of Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties in west-central Alabama on 27 April 2011, during the historic late-April 2011 tornado outbreak in the southeastern United States. According to official National Weather Service (NWS) documentation, the tornado was rated EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with a surveyed damage path length of 72.13 mi (116.1 km) and a maximum path width of 1,760 yd (1.0 mi). The event caused severe damage to homes, businesses, community facilities, and forested areas along its route and resulted in seven fatalities and fifty injuries. [1][2][9]

The tornado is named for the communities of Sawyerville in Hale County and Eoline in Bibb County, which experienced some of the most intense damage, including destruction of residential structures and the local fire department in Eoline. The NWS Birmingham office lists the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado among the significant tornadoes of 27 April 2011, a day on which numerous strong and violent tornadoes affected Alabama. The Alabama Tornado Database for 2011 includes a distinct entry for this tornado, documenting its EF3 rating, multi-county track through Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties, and associated casualties. [1][2][9]

title: Meteorological synopsis
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado formed within a broader episode of severe convective storms on 27 April 2011, when a powerful storm system produced numerous tornadoes across Alabama and surrounding states. The NWS Birmingham office’s event overview for the "Historic Outbreak of April 27, 2011" documents a series of tornadoes in central Alabama on that date, including long-track, strong, and violent tornadoes associated with supercell thunderstorms. Within this sequence, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is catalogued as an EF3 tornado affecting Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties, with an extended track and substantial casualty figures. [1][2][9]

According to the NWS damage survey specific to the event, the tornado touched down in far southwestern Greene County near the Tombigbee River just west of Tishabee, then moved northeast across rural portions of the county north of Forkland. The survey reports that the tornado subsequently crossed the Black Warrior River into Hale County, west of Sawyerville, and intensified as it approached and crossed Alabama Route 14 north of Sawyerville, reaching EF3 intensity with estimated winds of about 145 mph (233 km/h). As the tornado progressed through Hale County, it crossed local roads including County Roads 18, 21, and 29 and Alabama Highway 69, producing extensive structural damage and numerous casualties. [1][2][9]

Continuing northeastward, the tornado entered the Talladega National Forest near the community of Ingram and tracked toward the Bibb County line, where it caused widespread tree damage consistent with its strong intensity. In Bibb County, the tornado moved through the Eoline area, where the NWS survey describes significant structural damage characteristic of EF3 intensity, with winds again estimated near 145 mph. In Eoline, numerous mobile homes and single-family residences sustained minor to major damage, a dozen such structures were destroyed, and community facilities including the Eoline Fire Department and a nearby business were demolished. The survey notes that the tornado weakened slightly to EF2 intensity with estimated winds near 125 mph (201 km/h) as it crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton; several additional mobile homes and homes were heavily damaged or destroyed near County Road 26, and thousands of trees were downed along the later portion of the path before the tornado dissipated just northeast of Marvel. [1][2][9]

The Alabama Tornado Database for 2011 and the NWS event overview both list the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado with a total path length of approximately 72.13 mi and a maximum width of about 1,760 yd, underscoring its status as one of the longer-track tornadoes of that day in central Alabama. The tabular database provides the tornado’s date, time, counties affected, EF rating, path statistics, and casualty totals, while the narrative survey adds detailed geographic and intensity information along the track. [1][2][9]

title: Impact and damage
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado produced severe and varied impacts along its multi-county path, including extensive structural and vegetation damage and multiple casualties. The NWS Birmingham damage survey and the Alabama Tornado Database both attribute seven fatalities and fifty injuries to this tornado, distributed among Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties. The NWS overview of the "Historic Outbreak of April 27, 2011" also lists these casualty figures for the event in its tabular summary of the day’s tornadoes. [1][2][9]

In Greene County, the tornado initially struck rural areas near the Tombigbee River just west of Tishabee, moving northeast across sparsely populated terrain north of Forkland. The survey notes that at least four mobile homes, three outbuildings, and two churches were damaged or destroyed in this segment of the track, and two minor injuries were reported. Although the early portion of the path affected fewer structures than later segments, the damage to small community facilities and residences in Greene County illustrates the breadth of impacts even at lower population density. [1][2][9]

Upon crossing the Black Warrior River into Hale County, west of Sawyerville, the tornado encountered more developed areas and intensified as it crossed Alabama Route 14 north of Sawyerville, reaching EF3 strength with estimated winds near 145 mph. In this region, the tornado passed over and near local roads including County Roads 18, 21, and 29 and Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, generating extensive structural damage. The NWS survey reports that at least forty injuries and six fatalities occurred in Hale County as homes and other buildings were destroyed or heavily damaged along this part of the track. Thousands of trees were also uprooted or snapped, reflecting the strength and breadth of the circulation. [1][2][9]

The tornado’s impacts continued into Bibb County, where it moved through the Talladega National Forest near Ingram and then into the Eoline area. In forested sections, the survey describes significant tree damage, while in Eoline the tornado again produced EF3-level destruction, with winds estimated near 145 mph. Numerous mobile homes and single-family houses in Eoline sustained damage ranging from minor to major, and about a dozen such structures were destroyed outright. Community infrastructure in Eoline was also affected: the Eoline Fire Department building and another nearby business were destroyed when the tornado passed through the area. The survey documents one fatality in a vehicle near the fire department and at least ten other injuries in Bibb County, underscoring the localized severity of the event. [1][2][9]

Farther along its path, as the tornado crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton, it weakened to EF2 intensity with estimated winds near 125 mph but continued to inflict major damage on several mobile homes and single-family residences near County Road 26. Thousands of additional trees were downed along the later portion of the track before the tornado lifted just northeast of Marvel, at the northeastern end of its surveyed path. Across all three counties, the combination of residential, commercial, community-facility, and forest damage, together with the documented casualty figures, mark the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as one of the more destructive EF3 events of the April 27 outbreak in central Alabama. The available NWS and database sources do not provide a specific monetary estimate of economic losses for this tornado, so the financial impact can only be inferred from the documented extent of structural and vegetation damage. [1][2][9]

title: Aftermath and response
content:
Published National Weather Service documentation and the Alabama Tornado Database primarily focus on the meteorological characteristics and direct impacts of the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, and they do not provide detailed narrative accounts of the emergency response or long-term recovery specific to this event. Academic and public-health analyses of the broader April 27, 2011 Alabama tornado outbreak, which include this tornado among many others, describe coordinated emergency medical response and public-safety actions across the state but generally treat the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as part of the aggregate of storms rather than as a separate case study. In these sources, local emergency services, hospitals, and public-health agencies are reported to have managed large numbers of injured persons and fatalities from multiple tornadoes on 27 April, including those in Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties. [1][2][9][11]

Because the available NWS and database materials emphasize meteorological surveys and damage statistics and the statewide mortality and outbreak studies synthesize impacts across many tornadoes, specific information on community-level rebuilding efforts, assistance programs, or memorials dedicated solely to the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is not documented in these sources. As a result, while it is clear from official records that emergency responders, medical personnel, and public agencies were engaged in managing the consequences of this tornado along with others in the outbreak, detailed accounts of the response and recovery in the individual communities of Sawyerville, Eoline, and nearby rural areas remain limited in the available non-Wikipedia documentation. title: Context within the 2011 Super Outbreak and data conflicts
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado occurred during the late-April 2011 tornado outbreak, often referred to as the 2011 Super Outbreak, which affected large portions of the central and eastern United States. Outbreak overviews from Grokipedia and Tornado Talk describe a multi-day sequence of severe thunderstorms and tornadoes from 25 to 28 April 2011, with 27 April representing the single most active and deadly day of the event. Both sources identify Alabama as one of the states hardest hit by strong and violent tornadoes on 27 April, with numerous long-track tornadoes causing widespread destruction and hundreds of fatalities. Within Alabama, the NWS Birmingham "Historic Outbreak of April 27, 2011" page similarly documents many tornadoes of EF2 intensity or greater, including the Sawyerville–Eoline EF3 tornado in Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties. [6][8][9][1][2]

Although Grokipedia and Tornado Talk agree on the exceptional severity of the 2011 Super Outbreak, their summary statistics differ slightly. Grokipedia reports that the outbreak produced about 362 tornadoes in total, whereas the Tornado Talk overview gives a figure of about 368 tornadoes, reflecting differences in data sources or counting methodology. For 27 April specifically, Grokipedia cites approximately 199 tornadoes, while Tornado Talk estimates about 224 tornadoes for that day. The two sources also report slightly different overall fatality totals, with Grokipedia giving about 321 deaths associated with the outbreak and Tornado Talk listing about 324 fatalities. Despite these minor discrepancies, both accounts consistently portray the outbreak as one of the most significant tornado events in U.S. history and emphasize the major role of Alabama tornadoes, including the Sawyerville–Eoline storm, in contributing to the high casualty and damage figures. [6][8][9][1][2]

The NWS Birmingham outbreak summary for 27 April 2011 provides a more localized operational perspective, listing the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado alongside other significant Alabama tornadoes in a tabular format that includes time, affected counties, EF rating, path length, maximum width, and casualty statistics. This official record aligns with the Alabama Tornado Database for 2011 in identifying the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as an EF3 event with a long track across three counties, seven fatalities, and fifty injuries, situating it among the more destructive but not highest-rated tornadoes (which included several EF4 and EF5 tornadoes) during the outbreak in central Alabama. title: Overview
content:
The 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was a long-track, violent tornado that struck portions of Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties in west-central Alabama on 27 April 2011, during the historic late-April 2011 tornado outbreak in the southeastern United States. According to official National Weather Service (NWS) documentation, the tornado was rated EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with a surveyed damage path length of 72.13 mi (116.1 km) and a maximum path width of 1,760 yd (1.0 mi). The event caused severe damage to homes, businesses, community facilities, and forested areas along its route and resulted in seven fatalities and fifty injuries. [1][2][9]

The tornado is named for the communities of Sawyerville in Hale County and Eoline in Bibb County, which experienced some of the most intense damage, including destruction of residential structures and the local fire department in Eoline. The NWS Birmingham office lists the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado among the significant tornadoes of 27 April 2011, a day on which numerous strong and violent tornadoes affected Alabama. The Alabama Tornado Database for 2011 includes a distinct entry for this tornado, documenting its EF3 rating, multi-county track through Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties, and associated casualties. [1][2][9]

title: Meteorological synopsis
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado formed within a broader episode of severe convective storms on 27 April 2011, when a powerful storm system produced numerous tornadoes across Alabama and surrounding states. The NWS Birmingham office’s event overview for the "Historic Outbreak of April 27, 2011" documents a series of tornadoes in central Alabama on that date, including long-track, strong, and violent tornadoes associated with supercell thunderstorms. Within this sequence, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is catalogued as an EF3 tornado affecting Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties, with an extended track and substantial casualty figures. [1][2][9]

According to the NWS damage survey specific to the event, the tornado touched down in far southwestern Greene County near the Tombigbee River just west of Tishabee, then moved northeast across rural portions of the county north of Forkland. The survey reports that the tornado subsequently crossed the Black Warrior River into Hale County, west of Sawyerville, and intensified as it approached and crossed Alabama Route 14 north of Sawyerville, reaching EF3 intensity with estimated winds of about 145 mph (233 km/h). As the tornado progressed through Hale County, it crossed local roads including County Roads 18, 21, and 29 and Alabama Highway 69, producing extensive structural damage and numerous casualties. [1][2][9]

Continuing northeastward, the tornado entered the Talladega National Forest near the community of Ingram and tracked toward the Bibb County line, where it caused widespread tree damage consistent with its strong intensity. In Bibb County, the tornado moved through the Eoline area, where the NWS survey describes significant structural damage characteristic of EF3 intensity, with winds again estimated near 145 mph. In Eoline, numerous mobile homes and single-family residences sustained minor to major damage, a dozen such structures were destroyed, and community facilities including the Eoline Fire Department and a nearby business were demolished. The survey notes that the tornado weakened slightly to EF2 intensity with estimated winds near 125 mph (201 km/h) as it crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton; several additional mobile homes and homes were heavily damaged or destroyed near County Road 26, and thousands of trees were downed along the later portion of the path before the tornado dissipated just northeast of Marvel. [1][2][9]

The Alabama Tornado Database for 2011 and the NWS event overview both list the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado with a total path length of approximately 72.13 mi and a maximum width of about 1,760 yd, underscoring its status as one of the longer-track tornadoes of that day in central Alabama. The tabular database provides the tornado’s date, time, counties affected, EF rating, path statistics, and casualty totals, while the narrative survey adds detailed geographic and intensity information along the track. [1][2][9]

title: Impact and damage
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado produced severe and varied impacts along its multi-county path, including extensive structural and vegetation damage and multiple casualties. The NWS Birmingham damage survey and the Alabama Tornado Database both attribute seven fatalities and fifty injuries to this tornado, distributed among Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties. The NWS overview of the "Historic Outbreak of April 27, 2011" also lists these casualty figures for the event in its tabular summary of the day’s tornadoes. [1][2][9]

In Greene County, the tornado initially struck rural areas near the Tombigbee River just west of Tishabee, moving northeast across sparsely populated terrain north of Forkland. The survey notes that at least four mobile homes, three outbuildings, and two churches were damaged or destroyed in this segment of the track, and two minor injuries were reported. Although the early portion of the path affected fewer structures than later segments, the damage to small community facilities and residences in Greene County illustrates the breadth of impacts even at lower population density. [1][2][9]

Upon crossing the Black Warrior River into Hale County, west of Sawyerville, the tornado encountered more developed areas and intensified as it crossed Alabama Route 14 north of Sawyerville, reaching EF3 strength with estimated winds near 145 mph. In this region, the tornado passed over and near local roads including County Roads 18, 21, and 29 and Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, generating extensive structural damage. The NWS survey reports that at least forty injuries and six fatalities occurred in Hale County as homes and other buildings were destroyed or heavily damaged along this part of the track. Thousands of trees were also uprooted or snapped, reflecting the strength and breadth of the circulation. [1][2][9]

The tornado’s impacts continued into Bibb County, where it moved through the Talladega National Forest near Ingram and then into the Eoline area. In forested sections, the survey describes significant tree damage, while in Eoline the tornado again produced EF3-level destruction, with winds estimated near 145 mph. Numerous mobile homes and single-family houses in Eoline sustained damage ranging from minor to major, and about a dozen such structures were destroyed outright. Community infrastructure in Eoline was also affected: the Eoline Fire Department building and another nearby business were destroyed when the tornado passed through the area. The survey documents one fatality in a vehicle near the fire department and at least ten other injuries in Bibb County, underscoring the localized severity of the event. [1][2][9]

Farther along its path, as the tornado crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton, it weakened to EF2 intensity with estimated winds near 125 mph but continued to inflict major damage on several mobile homes and single-family residences near County Road 26. Thousands of additional trees were downed along the later portion of the track before the tornado lifted just northeast of Marvel, at the northeastern end of its surveyed path. Across all three counties, the combination of residential, commercial, community-facility, and forest damage, together with the documented casualty figures, mark the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as one of the more destructive EF3 events of the April 27 outbreak in central Alabama. The available NWS and database sources do not provide a specific monetary estimate of economic losses for this tornado, so the financial impact can only be inferred from the documented extent of structural and vegetation damage. [1][2][9]

title: Aftermath and response
content:
Published National Weather Service documentation and the Alabama Tornado Database primarily focus on the meteorological characteristics and direct impacts of the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, and they do not provide detailed narrative accounts of the emergency response or long-term recovery specific to this event. Academic and public-health analyses of the broader April 27, 2011 Alabama tornado outbreak, which include this tornado among many others, describe coordinated emergency medical response and public-safety actions across the state but generally treat the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as part of the aggregate of storms rather than as a separate case study. In these sources, local emergency services, hospitals, and public-health agencies are reported to have managed large numbers of injured persons and fatalities from multiple tornadoes on 27 April, including those in Greene, Hale, and Bibb Counties. [1][2][9][11]

Because the available NWS and database materials emphasize meteorological surveys and damage statistics and the statewide mortality and outbreak studies synthesize impacts across many tornadoes, specific information on community-level rebuilding efforts, assistance programs, or memorials dedicated solely to the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado is not documented in these sources. As a result, while it is clear from official records that emergency responders, medical personnel, and public agencies were engaged in managing the consequences of this tornado along with others in the outbreak, detailed accounts of the response and recovery in the individual communities of Sawyerville, Eoline, and nearby rural areas remain limited in the available non-Wikipedia documentation. [1][2][9][11]
